messages.content: "416 :     public static boolean equals(double x, double y) {\n417 :         return (Double.isNaN(x) && Double.isNaN(y)) || x == y;\n418 :     }"

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The failing test testArrayEquals() tests the MathUtils.equals() method for double arrays, with a particular assertion that the method returns false when both compared elements are Double.NaN. According to the IEEE standard, NaN is not equal to any value, including itself, so the expected result is false.

Inspecting MathUtils.equals(double[], double[]) reveals it checks for nulls, length mismatch, then iterates over elements comparing each pair with MathUtils.equals(double, double). The MathUtils.equals(double, double) method returns true if both arguments are NaN (Double.isNaN(x) && Double.isNaN(y)), otherwise falls back to x == y. This means two NaNs are considered equal by this method.

Thus, the array equals method returns true when both arrays contain NaN at the same position. This contradicts the IEEE standard and the test case's assertion, which expects false.

The current bug report confirms that some equals methods return true for NaN inputs, contradicting IEEE. The test failure stems directly from this implementation.

The likely cause of the bug is that MathUtils.equals(double, double) returns true if both arguments are NaN, which is not IEEE compliant. The equals method for arrays relies on this behavior and thus also does not comply.

The recent bug reports are unrelated to this issue.

Final conclusion: The MathUtils.equals(double, double) method violates the IEEE standard by returning true for Double.NaN arguments, causing the equals method for arrays to also disagree with the IEEE standard and fail the test.

This is the root cause of the test failure in testArrayEquals when comparing arrays containing NaN values.
